title: Hidden waves tens of metres tall travel through the ocean's interior
body: The ocean is layered, with lighter water lying on top of colder, denser water. When tides push water back and forth across an undersea ridge, such as the one under Hawaiʻi, deep dense water is forced upward and then sinks back, setting off waves along those layers. These internal tides often lift and drop water inside the ocean by **tens of metres**, yet move the surface by only a few centimetres, which is why satellites must average years of measurements to map them. In the South China Sea, internal waves can [top 200 m in height](https://physicstoday.aip.org/news/internal-waves-in-the-south-china-sea).

left.label: Inside the ocean
left.text: Layers of water often rise and fall by tens of metres, and even more in a few places

right.label: At the surface
right.text: The sea moves just a few centimetres: invisible to a ship, but measurable from orbit

slides.heading: How a tide makes a hidden wave

steps.label: Tidal currents push water over a ridge
Deep, dense water is forced upward
Gravity tugs it back down, and up again
Waves spread out along the ocean's layers

slides.label: the height internal waves in the South China Sea can top
slides.text: They form as tides slosh through the Luzon Strait. Where they break, they stir up turbulence 10,000 times stronger than in the open ocean.

slides.prompt: Once an undersea ridge sets them off, how far can internal tides travel?
slides.detail: Around Hawaiʻi their crests are about 50 to 100 km apart. They are thought to help mix warm upper water with cold deep water, a key part of the ocean's overturning circulation.
